name: Multi-gas (4-gas) monitors
summary: A palm-sized meter that checks air for oxygen, flammable gas (%LEL), hydrogen sulphide and carbon monoxide and alarms at set levels; it warns, and never makes a tank or pit safe to enter.
uses: Shows oxygen (% by volume), flammable gas (%LEL), H2S and CO (ppm) at once, but sees only the gases it has sensors for (MSA 4XR)
No CO2 sensor on a 4-gas monitor (MSA 4XR lists none): CO2 needs its own detector, as it can kill while oxygen still reads normal (CGA SA-22)
%LEL is not % gas: 100% LEL of methane is 5% gas in air, so a 10% LEL alarm is 0.5% methane (MSA 4XR)
The LEL sensor needs over 10% oxygen and reads petrol vapour low; it isn't meant for vapour from liquids that flash above 38 °C, such as diesel and kerosene (MSA 4XR, RAE TN-156)
Sample from outside with a pump and hose, top, middle and bottom; wait 2 minutes plus 2 s per foot (30 cm) of hose for each reading (ISC FAQ)
It doesn't make a space safe: forced air controls a hazard but isn't counted as removing it, and entry still needs a watcher outside and a lifeline (OSHA 1910.146)
identify: A palm-sized box, often yellow or black, clipped to a belt or chest, with a gas inlet grille, a screen, flashing lights and a loud horn; brands include MSA Altair, Honeywell BW GasAlert, Industrial Scientific Ventis and MX, Dräger X-am and Blackline. Some have a pump and a hose for sampling a space from outside (ISC FAQ). The screen shows O2 in % by volume (about 20.9 in clean air), flammable gas in %LEL or % methane, and H2S and CO in ppm, often with peak, STEL and TWA values (ISC BUMP, MSA 4XR). Alarm points vary by maker and are adjustable, so read the unit or its calibration sheet: MSA ships O2 low 19.5 and high 23.0, LEL 10 and 20, H2S 10 and 15, CO 25 and 100 ppm (MSA 4XR); Honeywell's single-gas BW Clip units use O2 19.5 and 23.5, H2S 10 and 15, CO 35 and 200 (BW CLIP). OSHA counts air as hazardous below 19.5% or above 23.5% oxygen, or above 10% of the lower flammable limit (OSHA 1910.146). On an MSA Altair, an LEL reading of XXX or a locked LEL alarm means over 100% LEL: an explosion risk, get out; it resets only when switched off and on in fresh air (MSA 4XR). MSA shows a heart symbol when a sensor nears or reaches end of life (MSA 4XR). Marks for use in flammable air: cULus or CSA Class I Division 1, ATEX and IECEx Ex ia (BW CLIP).
test: A bump test, a short shot of test gas above the alarm points, proves the sensors and alarms respond, not that they read right; calibration against certified gas sets accuracy. ISEA, quoted by OSHA, says bump or calibration-check before each day's use, and fully calibrate or retire any meter that fails (OSHA SHIB). MSA recommends a daily bump, CCOHS ideally just before each use, and Industrial Scientific a monthly calibration (MSA 4XR, CCOHS CS PROGRAM, ISC FAQ). CSA C22.2 No. 152 wants the LEL sensor checked daily on known methane, reading within 0 to +20% (MSA 4XR). Bump again after a drop, a soaking, storage or high H2S (MSA 4XR); silicone sprays and lotions, lead and sulphur compounds poison the LEL sensor for good (ISC POISONS). On a found meter: switch on outdoors in clean air, never in the space; fresh-air setup zeroes the sensors and resets O2 to 20.8%, so bad air would then read safe (MSA 4XR). Look for sensor-error, end-of-life and battery alarms; a battery alarm means it has stopped sensing (MSA 4XR). Read the calibration date. Oxygen: on MSA's single-gas O2 unit, breathe on the inlet for 3 to 5 seconds and the reading should drop (MSA ALTAIR SINGLE). O2 cells can fail so they stop responding (ISHN BW 2007), so a normal 20.9% in clean air proves nothing until the reading drops on a breath or low-oxygen gas. LEL, H2S and CO sensors read zero in clean air alive or dead (ISC BUMP); without in-date test gas they are unproven (OSHA SHIB). An unbumped meter is a maybe, never an all-clear; a bumped one still doesn't make a space safe to enter.

decay.note: Cells commonly last 2–3 years, some newer 5–7 (MSA BLOG FIXED); O2 about 2, H2S and CO over 4, and aged O2 cells are a top failure (ISC O2 LIFE). A disposable BW Clip O2 keeps 6 months boxed (BW CLIP). Test gas expires (OSHA SHIB).

improvise: Nothing replaces a working meter for low oxygen, H2S, CO or methane: you can't see them, and H2S kills your sense of smell at 100 to 150 ppm (OSHA H2S). Better than nothing: a bump-tested single-gas monitor for its one gas, or a home CO alarm for CO only, which is slow (70 ppm takes 60 to 240 minutes to alarm) and is made for homes, not workplace limits (KIDDE COPDLG-CA). With no proven meter, treat every pit, tank, manhole, well pit and silo as deadly and stay out: OSHA requires the air to be tested with a calibrated direct-reading instrument before anyone enters (OSHA 1910.146). Work from outside. If someone must go in with a proven meter, blow fresh air in where they will be, and they wear a harness on a line, with an attendant outside who stays out (OSHA 1910.146). Forced air controls a hazard but OSHA doesn't count it as removing it, so keep testing while anyone is inside (OSHA 1910.146). Never go in after someone who has collapsed: more than 60% of confined-space deaths are would-be rescuers (NIOSH 86-110). A meter on your belt only warns: a lone worker at an oil tank hatch died on a day his multi-gas monitor logged oxygen as low as 7% (MMWR TANKS). Leave at the first alarm (CCOHS CS PROGRAM). Useless: your nose, a flame (never use one to look for gas, RBQ GAS), and an oxygen reading alone in a CO2 room (CGA SA-22).
